decisions.summary: A ready ruling exports L7R_LAND_READY; holding_with holds nothing for the ticks it names, so the push and the CI merge read the landing's own ruling; where the first pass did not rule, the push's step asks again (export_ready); the ruling never reads which task the mark names.
decisions.why: Measured that a first-pass-only fix lands nothing (the push re-asks the hold); carrying one ruling to all three askers is what makes the fix reach its stated case.

decisions.summary: The hold's one condition is edited in shared::speckit (holding_with) under make guard-edit, a labeled deviation from the launcher's file list; T97's shared/src/tree* and T82's files untouched.
decisions.why: The launcher's file list is not the GM's words; the edit sits where the rule actually lives (one rule, three callers) and touches no other open task's files. Implementation placement is not a fidelity question.

decisions.summary: Padding L7R_LAND_TICKS with the mark's task, and a new `l7r-gate land --held` verb, priced and not taken.
decisions.why: Design alternatives declined for stated correctness reasons (a padded TICKS would name a task the landing does not tick); nothing asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: land-alone step 2, under its lock taken first, commits plan.md, tasks.md and plan-review.json built from HEAD with only the landing tasks' pieces replaced (temporary index, commit-tree, compare-and-swap update-ref), working files untouched; step 3's own-files refusal passes over the sectioned files.
decisions.why: Implements the task's second half (T95, CLEAR, could not land alone because plan.md also held T82's and T97's unreviewed sections); dry run on the real T95 case measured the commit carrying only T95's pieces.

decisions.summary: The staging lives in scripts/land-alone.sh's Python (PYLIB), not the land crate, so one program holds the pieces' rule for staging and take-back.
decisions.why: Placement choice; no part of the request reaches it.

decisions.summary: Where git merge-file conflicts on a sectioned file at take-back (measured shape: a tick's archive meeting another task's edit of the next heading), the file is merged piece by piece; a piece both sides changed differently still conflicts and nothing moves, as before.
decisions.why: Needed for (2) to work on the shape measured; keeps the existing stop on a true conflict.

decisions.summary: The files-own test does not see a file written by a Python program (the event log names no file for it; T96, open) and takes an edit older than 7 days as landed (land-alone's existing LANDED_SINCE bound).
decisions.why: Adjudicated each part. Python writes: the file name is absent from the log until T96 lands, so the test cannot see it; the gap already governs every started task other than the mark's under 405 D4 and land-alone's existing own-files refusal, so T101 adds no new class of exposure, and the fix is an already-filed open task (T96). 7-day bound: it is land-alone's own existing bound, reused rather than introduced. Neither removes anything the GM asked for in 451, and neither guts D4's purpose for the work the log does attribute.

decisions.summary: Case 5's clock seam holds the timer's first reading behind a gate file. The first jump is written only once that reading is taken, so it lands inside the wait by a condition and not by the shell's timing.
decisions.why: This is the rule T99's line asks for ('wait on a condition, not a clock'), applied to the window that feature 169's eight jumps were betting on. It stays inside the suite.

decisions.summary: Each next jump waits for four of the timer's logged reads after the last one, so at least one tick falls between two jumps. Pacing ends once the run has started.
decisions.why: A condition replaces a 'sleep 0.15'. It makes the case hold under load, which is what T99 asks.

decisions.summary: Each jump is stamped before it is written, with bash's $EPOCHREALTIME and no fork of date.
decisions.why: This removes the shell lag that caused the red. It is a mechanism inside the asked fix.

decisions.summary: The full wait is pinned by the guard's own 'suspend detected' lines, with jump sizes B x 2^(k-1) decoded to name the latest jump seen. Two checks follow: the run starts at least IDLE_WAIT_S after that jump's stamp, and the timer reads its clock at least 24 times between seeing that jump and the run's start.
decisions.why: This restates case 5's property (a jump restarts the FULL wait) in the timer's own events rather than in slack. It is red first on HEAD under a shell lag and red on a broken guard, as T99's line requires.

decisions.summary: A decode check holds the reading itself: every line on the B grid, the jumps contiguous, and as many lines as the record's suspends. The suite goes from 34 to 37 checks.
decisions.why: Its only job is to make the requested check read the guard's log correctly. That is enforcement of what was asked, not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: The guard's code is not changed. Only the test file changes.
decisions.why: This is inside the brief, which allowed the guard to change only to expose a timestamp. No timestamp had to be exposed.

decisions.summary: The old 0.35 s slack is retired in favour of IDLE_WAIT_S as a hard floor. The jump size moves from 500 s to B x 2^(k-1) with B = 300 s, checked by arithmetic against IDLE_SUSPEND_S and IDLE_GIVE_UP_S.
decisions.why: These are the test's own GUESS constants, moved to serve the condition-based check. No research claim or map moves.

decisions.summary: The new check pins a full wait after the LAST JUMP THE TIMER LOGGED. It no longer implies that the run began after ALL eight jumps. A timer that detected only its first jump would pass, and the plan says so.
decisions.why: The old implication was a timing assumption: that the shell writes all eight jumps inside one wait. Under a lagging shell a sound timer correctly ends its wait between jumps (the measured 'sleep 1.0 s late' batch), so keeping that implication would keep the very false red T99 removes. The guard's contract (D3: a wall jump past the ticks restarts the wait) is pinned as before, and the plan measured that a non-restarting timer is red in every batch. The undetected-after-first timer is a hypothetical, not a known defect, so nothing defective is left.

decisions.summary: Case 7's upper bound on a condition wait is raised from 8 s to 90 s, after 3 of 64 HEAD copies under load went red. It is fixed in this task.
decisions.why: A found defect (a check refusing good work under load) is fixed as it is found, with the bound case 4b already holds. A green run pays nothing, so this does not narrow what was asked.

decisions.summary: Case 6's 'the losers deferred' went red in 1 of 64 copies at load 133.7. It is not fixed here: it is outside case 5 and its fix is a design choice. It is filed as T104, which lands before T22.
decisions.why: This narrows nothing T99 was asked for, because T99's line is case 5. The defect is not left: it is filed with a reason, a task id and an order, as FR-009 requires, and it lands before T22, the same point T99 lands before.

decisions.summary: The brief cited T76's red as case 5, but it was case 4b, and it was not reproduced in 472 copies. It is filed as T104, which lands before T22.
decisions.why: It is outside case 5, was never reproduced, and is filed with a reason, an id and an order. Nothing in what was asked is dropped.

decisions.summary: The plan labels T99 as not performance work.
decisions.why: This is the conservative direction under FR-013/SC-006: the label can only put T99 behind performance tasks, never ahead of them. It narrows no priority the GM set.

decisions.summary: (waits: <when>) is read only right after the id's bracketed tags, where [perf] is read, so prose quoting the clause waits on nothing
decisions.why: Parsing detail of how a task line states its wait. It narrows nothing asked and stops stray prose from holding a task.

decisions.summary: One wait reading applied in next_independent (free slot), next_performance (task-start's FR-013 picker and the Stop hook's performance-first) and the nothing-running fallback; a waiting performance task no longer triggers FR-013's refusal, its case 'read rather than escaped'
decisions.why: This narrows the accepted FR-013. That spec gives a performance task waiting on another's landing an escape of a recorded reason (FR-012, counted by SC-006), and the plan drops it from the refusal instead. The ruling is against the request ('prioritize performance improvements going forward'; measurement tasks 'counted as a performance task for the purpose of scheduling and coming first'). A performance task that cannot start yet cannot go first, and refusing other work for it idles builders, which defeats the purpose of making everything faster. FR-013's own wording names this exact case as a permitted exception. The reason is still recorded, in git, on the waiting task's committed line, not in the escape log. A startable performance task is refused exactly as before, so the enforcement stays real. Each form is ruled separately in D2a-D2d.

decisions.summary: Form 'T88 lands' / 'T02-T21 land': met when none of the named tasks is open
decisions.why: This is FR-013's named escape case word for word: a performance task waiting on another task's landing. It releases itself when the landing happens, and it is stated on the committed task line.

decisions.summary: T88's 'after T<n>' rule moved from the free slot into the shared reading, so it now also reaches the FR-013 picker and the nothing-running fallback
decisions.why: Same class as D2a: the task cannot start until T<n> is no longer open. Its reach grew to the picker, but its meaning did not change, and it releases itself when T<n> closes.

decisions.summary: Another open line's 'lands before T<n>' holds T<n> (4 open lines in 451 say 'lands before T22')
decisions.why: This is still 'waiting on another task's landing': another task has committed to land first, and 'lands before ...' is the ordering phrase this feature's own FR-009 requires. It is read from prose on a different line, unlike the positional clause, so a passing mention could hold a performance task. It fails toward hiding rather than starting, against the block's stated direction. But the hold ends when that line closes, so it never hides a task for good. Not a defect now: in 451 all 4 measured lines name T22 on purpose.

decisions.summary: Form 'a full day after T.. land(s)': met 24 h past the latest logged landing (land end lines, landed true); T22 a full day after T02-T21 (until 2026-11-22T08:00:27.560Z), T98 a full day after T88 (until 2026-11-22T18:40:27.980Z)
decisions.why: After the landing this is a clock, so it gets D7e's test. Unlike the bare date it is anchored to a logged landing, it has one fixed duration, and it is written on the committed line. A full day's measurement cannot be taken before that day has elapsed (SC-005: 'the first full day after landing'), so the rule is physically impossible to apply sooner, not merely awkward. The GM asked for measurement tasks to count as performance work, and a measurement task taken early measures nothing. T98's stated need is 'a night of rolling dispatch'. The night window cited was 07:50-17:30Z, and the next one after T88's 18:40Z landing is 2026-11-22 07:50-17:30Z. The 24 h hold ends at 18:40Z, about 1h10m after that window closes. So the convention holds T98 only a little longer than its need, and less than the rejected end-of-UTC-day form (00:00Z on 11-23) would. Not a defect.

decisions.summary: Anything else in the parentheses is no wait (fails toward a start the session sees named)
decisions.why: Unreadable text leaves the task inside FR-013's refusal, so this fails toward enforcement, not away from it.

decisions.summary: A bare date is not a form; pinned as no wait
decisions.why: This complies with the earlier plan-review ruling D7e (NOT LEGITIMATE), which this block records. With no form of wait unanchored to a landing, FR-013 is left whole.

decisions.summary: Tasks ticked before the log carried land end lines (451 T02-T05) count as landed long ago
decisions.why: Reads history the log cannot hold. Ticked tasks did land. The latest landing that matters, T11, is logged.

decisions.summary: T22 and T98 lines carry their waits clauses
decisions.why: This is the data the mechanism exists for. Both waits are anchored to logged landings, measured 2026-11-21.

decisions.summary: task_start.rs unchanged; it calls the shared next_performance
decisions.why: Implementation placement. The behavior change is ruled under D2.

decisions.summary: The free slot's PERF_LATER_OK reason now reads 'is started or touches a running task's files'
decisions.why: The message is reworded to match the narrower set of tasks it now covers. Nothing asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: L7R_WAITS_NOW as the tests' clock seam, else the system clock
decisions.why: Test seam following the L7R_PERMIT_NOW precedent. It acts only on a full-day wait already written on a committed line.

decisions.summary: performance() looks for the heading as text before running its pattern over plan.md
decisions.why: A CPU fix to a cost this change exposed (0.09-0.16 s back to 0.00-0.02 s, measured 2026-11-21). Within the performance work asked for.

decisions.summary: SC-006's count reads off the escape log; a start made while a performance task waits leaves no escape row; left because no SC-006 reader exists
decisions.why: The same narrowing as D2, seen from the spec's side. It is judged fresh, not on the block's appeal to 'T102's plan review notes', which nothing in this bundle backs. Under the defect test only a wrong outcome now is a defect. The block's grep (2026-11-21) finds no reader of 451's SC-006, so nothing misreads today and nothing defective is left. Record for whoever builds that reader or amends the spec: FR-013 and SC-006 still say 'recorded escape', but a waiting task's reason is now on its own line and in the land log, not in the escape log.

decisions.summary: After the date form was dropped, the three tests were rewritten to wait on landings and not rerun red
decisions.why: FR-012's red-first is owed for a refusal that fires, and T102 adds no new refusal: it makes existing ones skip a task that cannot start. The original tests were red on the unchanged hook (357/3, measured 2026-11-21). That the rewritten tests would still be red is argued, not measured: the unchanged hook does not read the clause at all, so its output cannot depend on what the clause says.

decisions.summary: Each of shape's strip patterns (HEREDOC, QUOTED_HEREDOC, UNQUOTED_HEREDOC on '<<', BACKTICK_SPAN on a backtick, INTERPRETER_C on a trimmed text ending in 'c') is searched only where its text holds the literal any match needs, reusing T97's shared::regex::Lazy; cut takes a Lazy.
decisions.why: This is what T103's line asks for (each strip gated on the literal a match needs, as T97 gated the walk's patterns, measured first). It is a [perf] task under FR-013, and the spec's 2026-11-20 request puts performance work first. No answer changes, only the builds.

decisions.summary: QUOTED is replaced by a linear scan (quoted_spans) that reads quoted strings the way the pattern did, with strip_quotes writing from the spans, because the backtracking pattern hung on an unclosed quote followed by many backslashes (corpus rows 3,148 and 7,510 under no_poll_hooks in the background).
decisions.why: A guard that hangs is a defect under constitution XIV's definition (a tool that hangs), and T103 found it in its own file. The fix-as-we-go rule has a known defect fixed before moving on. A pattern replaced by a scan builds no pattern at all, which also serves the line's purpose of no pattern build where none is needed. The differential test (scan equals find_iter on all texts up to 7 characters) is the plan's own evidence that the scan does the pattern's job. No reviewer imposed it as an exactness standard, and it enforces the requested behavior rather than adding scope.

decisions.summary: tree.rs:348's own '<<' gate before strip_heredocs, now redundant, is left as it stands (outside T103's files).
decisions.why: A redundant check that still answers correctly is a difference, not a defect (constitution XIV v2.36.0), so leaving it narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.summary: The same QUOTED pattern text at wait.rs:53 and house_style_hooks.rs:85 is not fixed here: it is outside T103's files and neither copy was measured to hang. It is filed as T108 [perf], which measures first whether each copy hangs on row 3,148's shape and then gives each T103's scan as one shared function. T108 lands before T22.
decisions.why: T103's line covers shared::shape's strips, not the other modules' copies, so deferring them does not narrow what T103 was asked to do. The deferral is in FR-009's form: why it is not fixed here, the filed task id (T108, confirmed on tasks.md line 92) and its order ('lands before T22'). No hang is measured in either copy, so no known defect is carried past this step, and T108 is filed to measure it first rather than assume it.

decisions.summary: Build-count pins (shape/tests/builds.rs, quotes.rs, run as child processes printing regex::BUILT) on plain, redirected, backtick, quoted, -c and heredoc commands, plus a 10 s deadline pin on an unclosed quote before forty escapes, each red first against the snapshot.
decisions.why: FR-012 red first, and the line asks for a build-count test red first. These tests only fail when the requested gating, or the hang fix, is missing: they enforce the request and add nothing to its scope.

decisions.summary: Touches only shape.rs and shape/. Nothing of T99's or T102's files. T96's clippy errors in tree/program/tests.rs, which turned closing-checks run 1 RED, are left as T96's.
decisions.why: Keeping to the task's own files narrows nothing asked of T103. The red lint belongs to another task's file and is recorded as BLOCKED on T96, not waved off as T103's.

decisions.summary: An arbiter accept clears only the owed/BLOCKED blocks inside the sections of the tasks its trigger names (round trigger #<task>, or the ask subject's task ids via named_tasks), plus their removed blocks; a block outside every named span is not cleared. Scope is read from the trigger, never the question's prose.
decisions.why: A defect fix (fix as we go; constitution XIV's 'a check that passes bad work'): measured 2026-11-21, four accepts cleared 28, 10, 9 and 2 blocks outside the asked task's section, including T76's and T77's unreviewed changes. The rulings themselves scope the accept to the asked task ('This accept stands as the verdict of T79's plan review on the section as it reads now'; T67's and T33's likewise), and FR-043 keeps the verdict per block, so a task round's accept covering only that task's blocks implements what the arbiter ruled and narrows nothing the GM asked.

decisions.summary: An accept whose trigger names no task (5 of 21 accepted plan asks, measured) clears the whole plan as before.
decisions.why: Keeps the existing behavior for asks whose subject was the plan (e.g. ask:420-plan-round3, whose ruling is 'The plan stands as it reads now'); the question was the plan, so the whole plan is its verdict's scope.

decisions.summary: A named task with no section in plan.md or plan-done.md: the whole plan's scope, as plan decided (decision_refusal) reads such a task.
decisions.why: This is the one arm that keeps whole-plan clearing for a named task, and it is not the defect surviving. A task with no section anywhere has no blocks of its own, so its decisions can only be in the plan-stage blocks, and plan decided (decision_refusal) already reads it that way. For such a task the question put to the arbiter was the plan, so the accept's scope matches the question. The over-clearing the section fixes happened only where the named task HAD a section and blocks outside it were cleared too, and D1 ends that.

decisions.summary: A named task whose section is archived (plan-done.md only): nothing recorded, never the whole plan.
decisions.why: FR-044: no review reads plan-done.md and a removed section owes no review, so there is nothing to record; refusing to fall back to the whole plan prevents the over-clearing this task fixes.

decisions.summary: Labeled CONVENTION: the trigger is the scope source because its subject is already a machine-read id (the GM 2026-10-25, the algorithmically easier route where the record is silent).
decisions.why: A mechanism choice inside the fix, applying a standing GM rule; it decides no question the request or rulings settle differently.

decisions.summary: Each named task's tasks.<id> is written CLEAR, declared round-arbiter, at its section digest, with the replaced reviewer entry kept as accepted_over; the tick, push, plan decided and T84's builder-stop guard read that one entry.
decisions.why: Feature 409 (an ask with REVIEW=plan stands as the plan review's verdict) and each cited ruling ('this accept is the plan review's verdict on T67's plan section') require the accept to BE the task verdict; measured 2026-11-21 the store held T33, T46, T67 and T79 BLOCKED though each landed on an accept - a gate reading wrong. Writing it fixes that defect.

decisions.summary: make arbiter-ruled names the scope, each heading recorded CLEAR and the task verdict; a batch's plan accept (BATCH=1) is applied as a single ruling's is.
decisions.why: The output change makes the fix visible where a bare count hid 28 blocks; the batch path recording a plan accept but never applying it is a found defect (observed 2026-11-21 by grep -rn arbiter_accept rust/), fixed here as fix-as-we-go requires.

decisions.summary: The unreviewed changes the over-broad accepts cleared (T56 log path, T77 filing named, T76 make events-refile now takes FROM=) are ruled within and not re-reviewed, T76 being landed and archived.
decisions.why: This ruling is the reviewer's own, not the author's 'Ruled here', and it rests on the before/after fragments the section quotes, not on the blocks' full text, which the bundle does not carry. The section's counts check out (28 = 2 + T76's and T77's 2 + 24 templates; 10 = 2 + 1 + 7; 9 = 2 + 7). On those fragments: T56's log path and T77's naming its filed task are typo-scale. T76's change wires its own tool's FROM= argument into its own make target, which is within its task, narrows nothing and leaves no wrong outcome. T76's section is in plan-done.md, which FR-044 says no review reads.

decisions.summary: Left: task_refusal's deferral arm (the decide lint, a separate check), and the four stale BLOCKED entries in plan-review.json, not hand-edited.
decisions.why: Neither is a defect under constitution XIV: the deferral arm is a different check this task does not touch, and the four entries' sections are archived, so nothing that gates reads them (plan decided finds no section). No request clause asks for either.

decisions.summary: Performance work? no.
decisions.why: T92 fixes plan-review record keeping: what an arbiter accept clears and writes. It neither saves time nor measures where time goes, so neither FR-013 nor the GM's 2026-11-20 widening to measurement work ('this kind of measurement task ... counted as a performance task') reaches it.

decisions.summary: Order: before T22, as its line says; beside T96 and T103, whose files it leaves.
decisions.why: Fix as we go: a known defect in the review gate is fixed before the next step. Sitting beside T96 and T103 is file-disjoint scheduling and defers nothing.

decisions.summary: Replace the three copies of the backtracking quoted-string pattern in wait.rs and house_style_hooks.rs (cond_grammar's QUOTED, masked's QUOTED_SPAN, the held re-call shape) with shape::quoted_spans, made pub and must_use, nothing else of shape.rs changed
decisions.why: T108 is a [perf] task under FR-013 (a hook hang stalls the builders' loop), filed from T103's Found and left, so it falls under the GM's 2026-11-20 ask to prioritize performance work. The fix removes an exponential search, which is what the task is for. It narrows nothing that was asked.

decisions.why: An implementation choice that keeps the guard doing its job on the same calls. It neither narrows nor adds to the request.

decisions.summary: Three hang pins, red first: wait's in T103's child-process form with a 10 s deadline (GUESS), and house style's two under the module's 30 s CPU bound (T81, CONVENTION). Both deadlines reused as they stand
decisions.why: FR-012's red-first form. These are tests that fail only if the hang the task fixes comes back, so they enforce the task rather than add scope.

decisions.summary: Three exhaustive differential tests (55,987 / 55,987 / 66,430 texts, counts that follow from the alphabets and lengths) hold each new reading to the pattern it replaced, and a replay of T93's 9,646 commands shows 0 changed verdicts
decisions.why: This is evidence that the guards still do their job (the sheets a check passed still pass), which the GM's 2026-11-18 rule says is owed for a changed check. It is not offered as a requirement that bytes must match: the plan treats no difference as a stop and asks for no ruling on one. It is verification of the requested fix, not new scope.

decisions.summary: Touch only wait.rs, house_style_hooks.rs, their tests and shape.rs, and nothing of T96's (shared::tree, event_log_hooks) or T92's (the arbiter and plan crates)
decisions.why: Coordination between concurrent tasks. Every copy left out is filed below with an order, so nothing the request or spec requires is dropped.

decisions.summary: The same pattern in T96's tree.rs:70 QUOTED and tree/program.rs:63 TRIPLE, and tree::walk's hang on a plain command (house style still holds past 10 s on that shape after T108), left to T112, which lands before T22
decisions.why: A found-and-left item in FR-009's form: the reason (T96's builder has live uncommitted work in both files), the filed task id and its order ('lands before T22'). The defect is filed as performance work, so FR-013 schedules it first, and it is not carried past a next step. The Approach's goal states the remaining plain-command hang honestly instead of claiming it fixed. The spec requires no fix in this task, so nothing is narrowed.

decisions.summary: The same pattern in make_only_hooks.rs:125, no_poll_hooks/pace.rs:36 and readme_hooks.rs:51 left to T113, which waits on no task and lands before T22. The class census is stated with its method (two greps over rust/, every hit read)
decisions.why: Again in FR-009's form: reason, id and order, plus the 'how every instance was found' line FR-009 asks for when a fix names a class. Splitting the work into a separately filed perf task, which FR-013 puts first, ordered before the next step, does not narrow what the GM asked or what the spec requires.

decisions.summary: After two closing runs went RED only on make static's format check, a third make static was refused by FR-007's guard, so the crate-scoped format check (exit 0) stands for it, with lint, tests and cover clean before a whitespace-only rustfmt rewrap
decisions.why: FR-007 refuses a third make static and names the crate-scoped checks as the compliant command. The GM approved exactly that (improvement 2: crate-scoped checks while iterating). The landing's own gate still runs in full, so following the spec's own guard narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The fix waits on T96, then T110; T49 lands on its own as gate-write's half of T110's reading.
decisions.why: This sets the order and narrows nothing: the defect is still fixed in full, after the two tasks it depends on.

decisions.summary: The parameter-binding and root-joining reading lives only in shared::tree::program (T110), and gate-write builds no second copy.
decisions.why: This decides where the code lives. The outcome named in Approach item 1 is unchanged.

decisions.summary: A literal binds, by position or keyword, to a parameter of a function defined once. A *args parameter or a second def binds nothing.
decisions.why: This is the gate's rule that a path it cannot resolve fails open: with a second def it is not statically known which body runs. For *args the binding is knowable, so leaving it out is a gap. The reviewer measured on 2026-11-21 with /tmp/fid-t49/star.py (heredocs and python -c; a def with a starred parameter, called anywhere with a string literal, whose body holds a write or copy/replace sink): 0 in T93's corpus and 0 in T33's fixtures. This is a gap with no occurrence, not a known defect left.

decisions.why: The instrument could have seen the other sinks: /tmp/t49/scripts/measure.py's sinks() searches os.replace/os.rename/shutil.copy*/move (form 4) and os.remove/unlink (form 5). The reviewer re-ran it on 2026-11-21 on both corpora and got forms {0:36, 1:9} on T93's corpus and {0:9, 1:78, 3:7} on the fixtures, so 0 of forms 4 and 5 in either. That makes this a gap with no occurrence, not a known defect left (constitution XIV v2.36.0). The three forms hold every observed hit.

decisions.summary: A literal is joined onto a root by ROOT / P, os.path.join(ROOT, P) or ROOT + P, where ROOT is a top-level name bound once to a literal.
decisions.why: This carries T49's line (#170's shape, R = pathlib.Path(...)) and T110's '+' form.

decisions.summary: An f-string root (window#72) stays let through.
decisions.why: T49's own line, as quoted in item 2, says 'a base the program computes fails open, so window#72 stays let through'.

decisions.summary: Eight fixed sleeps in four other hook suites, plus test-finished-run-hooks.sh's settle, wait for an event the next check needs, so a slow host fails good work there too. They are not fixed here: filed as T115, lands before T22.

The ruling relies on the second half of the why: each suite owes its own red-first run (FR-012's discipline, as T111's runs here show), which is a separate measured job per suite, not an awkwardness. The first half (the launcher scoped T111 to this suite) is a session's scoping and is given no weight. The purpose of improvement 4 (fewer plan re-rounds through fixing in the task) is not gutted: the defect is filed with a fixed order, not left open-ended.

decisions.summary: Six lines whose checks assert that nothing happened, or whose sleep cannot change the verdict, are listed but not filed: idle-tests 73, 182, 191, 217 and closing-checks 112, 115.

None of the six refuses good work, and none reads the wrong process. Line 104 did read the wrong process: under load it inspected the pre-exec copy of the suite and could pass whatever the hook did. None of the six is a wrong outcome under XIV v2.36.0, so leaving them narrows nothing.

decisions.id: T51-d2 make-only's unread route an accepted limitation
decisions.summary: Make-only gains the script route only if the post-T118 replay shows a correction (none in either corpus; 17 of 17 guard-file script writes carried GUARD_EDIT_OK), so its unread route is an accepted limitation; the cost named is that an unescaped script write of a guard file would pass unrecorded.
decisions.why: The block's own cost sentence describes a check that passes bad work: a script that writes a guard file with no escape gets past make-only's guard-write. That is a wrong outcome by XIV's definition, and it can be reproduced on demand from one constructed fixture. Corpus silence does not change that. The block is inconsistent here: item 12 treats gate-write's 'would-be and not observed' hole as worth fixing and make-only's identical hole as acceptable. The argument against landing now (16 false refusals) runs out at T118: by the block's own breakdown, 12 of the 16 are t67's run argv lists and 3 are joined reads (window#305, #306, #309), both shapes T118 teaches. That leaves 1 (t58's path-prefix filter). The condition 'only if the replay shows a correction' is set against the same corpora that showed none, so as written it settles the question rather than asking it again after T118. Leaving a known defect needs a filed id and an order (FR-009); this one has neither. What it should say instead: at T51's post-T118 replay, make-only also gains the script route. Its correction is shown red-first by a fixture, a script that writes a guard file with no escape, which make-only must refuse. Any false refusals that remain (the path-prefix shape) are fixed in T51's files or filed with 'lands before T51', under item 7's own rule that a shape is never landed as a limit. decisions.id: T115-D7 no-poll suite flake filed as T139

The defect is not carried forward: FR-009's three parts are present (why it is not fixed here, the filed id T139, and the order 'lands before T22'), which honors fix-as-we-go before the next step.

decisions.summary: T115 is classed as not performance work (a test's correctness under load), with suite timings recorded as a side effect.
decisions.why: FR-013 and the GM's 2026-11-20 and 2026-11-21 words make performance and measurement tasks first. A fix to tests failing good work under load is neither, and the GM's closing-checks filing concerned a different task. The classification narrows nothing asked.

decisions.summary: No map changes; only the five suites and this section are touched, nothing of T118, T89 or T129; the suites' timings are recorded old against new, within the load's spread.

decisions.why: T94 fixes test isolation and the guard log's fixture rows. It does not measure where time goes, which is the measurement work the GM's 2026-11-20 words put first.

Default-fix-in-task (improvement 4) is a default, and FR-009 is the accepted spec's allowance for this exception. Filing the leaks as one bundled task matches the GM's 2026-11-22 bundling words. They are bundled with the other test-log leaks under the GM's 2026-11-22 bundling approval, and ordered before T22, so they are not left without a home. I took T143 and its order on the block's word.

decisions.summary: A name assigned more than once in straight-line code is one binding: each bare assignment renamed, each read bound to the last assignment before it, a read before any assignment the environment's value or empty.
decisions.why: This is what T91's line asks for (a straight-line reassignment reads its last value). It is a fix of a check refusing good work, which constitution XIV and the fix-as-we-go rule ask to be fixed.

decisions.summary: A read whose last assignment follows && or ||, or that stands after a branch, a loop, a function or a source, keeps HEAD's reading at each value. Widening the rule to && was priced and not taken.
decisions.why: None of these is straight-line code, which is what T91's line names. An assignment after && or || may not run, so the read may see the earlier value, and judging each value is the correct answer there, not an over-refusal. No mirror refusal is lost. The moved pin's && form agrees: its last assignment follows a ;.

decisions.id: D-a (opaque forms in the stretch, filed as T145)
decisions.summary: A backtick, $(, brace group, comment or ${X:-$(...)} between the last assignment and the read keeps HEAD's reading at each value, so a scratch write that bash makes is still refused there. Filed as T145, which lands before T140.
decisions.why: This narrows T91's line, because these commands are straight-line code and the leftover over-refusal is a defect (a check refusing good work). The plan's stated reason, that bind.rs's flat scanner would need to parse substitution bodies, comments and brace groups, is a cost and does not make it legitimate by itself. What does is this: the defect is not dropped but sequenced, filed as T145 to land before T140, the task that waits on T91. So no known defect is carried into the next step, which is what fix-as-we-go asks. The GM's own words of 2026-11-22 are that tasks keep being filed at the current rate and are bundled when fixed, so filing a sibling task departs from no instruction. The deferral also carries FR-009's why, id and order. T91's purpose is met: ordinary straight reassignments are read as bash reads them. The exception errs only toward HEAD's refusal, and the either-end pin holds it there.

decisions.summary: A name read through ${D:=W}, ${D:-W} or ${D-W} is not taken as Straight and falls back to HEAD's reading at each value (added on T91's first plan review).
decisions.why: This prevents a regression the first cut introduced: a mirror write read as elsewhere. Keeping a mirror value at either end refused is in T91's line, and the exclusion only returns a name to HEAD's reading.

decisions.summary: The single many-valued name of a command is judged value by value up to 128 values. Past 128 it falls back to T79's unknown reading.
decisions.why: T91's line asks that a lone loop past the 64 cap be judged value by value, and the plan bounds that at 128. Some bound is physically required, because a guard that runs on every Bash call has to finish in bounded time: measured, 128 values cost 44.7 ms and 256 cost 171 ms (2026-11-22, T83's timer). The fallback is the conservative one (refuse, never under-refuse). The measured corpora hold no lone loop past 64 at all, so the bound defeats no case the purpose covers. The constant is labeled a CONVENTION.

decisions.summary: A command with several many-valued names keeps MAX_BINDINGS = 64 and T79's unknown reading, unchanged.
decisions.why: T91's line names a lone loop. Products of names are outside it, and the plan leaves them exactly as HEAD has them.

decisions.id: D-b gate-write's 7 product refusals not judged
decisions.summary: Whether gate-write's 7 refusals of over-cap product rows are right is left unjudged.
decisions.why: These rows are outside T91's line and unchanged from HEAD. No defect is established, so nothing is being deferred.

decisions.summary: Loop values are deduplicated by text, and bindings skips a name already bound.
decisions.why: These are mechanics of (b), and they change no verdict in the replay.

decisions.summary: The && form of a_name_assigned_from_pwd_is_where_the_shell_stands_then now reads elsewhere, as bash writes it. Its ; variant keeps clone and elsewhere.
decisions.why: This is a correction that follows directly from (a): bash writes there.

decisions.id: Found and left: T144 (${D:-W} and ${D:+W} default dropped)
decisions.summary: A defect that predates T91 (T79): replaced() drops the :- and :+ operand, so a mirror write can be read as elsewhere. Filed as T144, which lands before T140.
decisions.why: This is a defect left, and the more serious kind: a check passing bad work, because a mirror write can be read as elsewhere. It is ruled LEGITIMATE on the same ground as T145. It is not dropped: it is filed as T144 to land before T140, the next task that depends on this one, so it is not carried into the next step, and FR-009's why, id and order are all present. It predates T91 (it is T79's). T91's fix reads it exactly as HEAD does, because the default and assign ops are excluded from Straight, so T91 neither causes it nor makes it worse. Fixing it needs tree.rs's expand, which lies outside T91's bind rule. That last point is the plan's stated reason, not the ground for this ruling.

decisions.summary: The task is classed as not performance work.
decisions.why: This is a guard correctness fix. The cost measurement shows no rise (0.06% fewer instructions on ux).

decisions.summary: On a build error holding `undefined hidden symbol`, drop only the incremental session holding each `.rcgu.o` unit the linker names and that crate's `.fingerprint/<crate>-<meta>`, under cargo's own lock, print what was dropped, and rebuild once incrementally
decisions.why: This is the task line's own remedy, 'dropping that crate's incremental session', as the block quotes it. The fingerprint drop is what makes the heal work: 449 T244 cleared sessions but not fingerprints, cargo kept the broken rlib as fresh, and the scratch copy showed a stale rlib behind an out-of-date fingerprint recompiled and linked clean (e2e.log, 8.3 s). Its reach is no wider than the directories the linker names.

decisions.summary: A link error that names no unit rebuilds once with CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0; a second failure is refused as before, with the cargo text
decisions.why: A bounded fallback inside the same goal: a gate command that failed on stale link state runs on a freshly linked tool. It adds no behavior beyond one retry and keeps the existing refusal afterwards. In this path the stale incremental set is left as it is (the block's own finding is that a CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 set is separate), so goal 1's 'next incremental build links with no retry' is guaranteed only for the named-unit path. That is a limit of a fallback for unrecognised failures and no narrowing of the task.

decisions.summary: An uncompiling file is still refused with no retry (T41 kept); only the link-error text triggers a retry
decisions.why: Keeps existing, separately approved behavior that T142's line does not ask to change; the detection is limited to rust-lld's own spelling.

decisions.summary: Always-non-incremental and `lto = "off"` rejected: T95's incremental tool profile and default ThinLTO kept
decisions.why: Leaves T95's measured, GM-asked profile as it is. The alternative was measured to cost 83-116 s per rebuild of the core crates against about 5 s (time.sh, measured 2026-11-22), which works against the feature's performance purpose. Keeping an approved profile is no narrowing.

decisions.summary: Show the rust-lld lines and a line naming what was dropped, not the full link command line
decisions.why: Presentation of the refusal and the heal. It serves the defect statement in Approach item 12, where a wall of linker text is the symptom.

decisions.summary: Change only scripts/gates/l7r-gate.sh, its hook test and this section; the real cache is never removed by hand; red-first test (FR-012)
decisions.why: Matches T142's line and FR-012's red-first requirement (13 FAIL lines on HEAD's launcher, then green, measured 2026-11-22).

decisions.summary: The same stale-link exposure in scripts/hooks/l7r-guard.sh (l7r_guard, same incremental tool profile, l7r_shared units that failed l7r-rust twice) and in make rust-test's dev-profile builds is deferred to T146, which lands before T98
decisions.why: The fix stops at the gate launcher although the same defect class is known in two other builds, so this is a narrowing, and it is a defect left rather than a difference. It is legitimate because the defect is not left: it is filed as T146 with a stated order (before T98, whose occupancy measurement a stalled build would skew). It also states why it is not fixed here (T142's line is the gate launcher's failure, and the guard fails open to its last good binary rather than refusing every gate command). FR-009 asks for exactly those three things: a reason, a filed id and an order. Nothing the GM asked is excepted: the request does not name this defect, and the GM's 2026-11-22 words favour filing small defects and bundling them over widening one task. One caution for T146: these two instances came from a scan of transcripts for link failures, which finds builds that FAILED, not every build exposed. T146's census should be drawn from the launchers that build with CARGO_INCREMENTAL or the tool or dev profile, for example a grep over scripts/ and the Makefiles, and not from this list.

decisions.summary: make task-start, make closing-checks and make decide take T=a,b,c as make land already does; a bundle gets one section and one verdict that counts for each task.
decisions.why: This is how the GM's 2026-11-22 request is carried out: bundle the open small tasks and work them at the same time, which he approved with 'so let's do that then'.

decisions.summary: active-task names the first member as task and every member as tasks. Each member's start is logged, the first member's last, so it is the task in force. All of a bundle's refusals are checked before anything is written.
decisions.why: This is how a bundle is started. A single task's flow is unchanged (Approach 1, 12).

decisions.summary: A member is refused when its box is not open, when it is a phase task (a parked stage's task included) or when its feature is held. The plan has no size test, so which tasks to bundle is the caller's choice.
decisions.why: The GM's words leave it to the session to look at the open tasks and pick the tiny ones, so leaving out a size test narrows nothing. A phase task is a stage of a staged plan, not one of the small defects the GM asked to bundle. A held feature or a closed box cannot be started alone either.

decisions.summary: Performance-first is checked for each member. A member that is not performance work is refused while an open performance task waits, unless that waiting task is a member of the same bundle. A performance task waiting outside the bundle still causes the refusal, with the same escape a single start has.
decisions.why: This is an exception to FR-013's literal start refusal. The GM's own words imply it: look at 'what set of tasks is currently open' and work them 'at the same time'. If the exception were refused, the performance member would have to go alone first, and every member would pay the fixed cost again, which is exactly what bundling exists to stop. It leaves FR-013's purpose intact, which is that performance work comes first and makes everything after it faster. The block says members are 'started, closed and landed together' and 'the landing ticks every member'. So a member that is not performance work can never land ahead of the performance member it shares a bundle with, and the end-to-end pin (land/tests/bundle.rs) lands the bundle as one unit. Counting each member as started for land-alone (T101) only lets the bundle land apart from other tasks. It does not let one member land apart from its own bundle. Any performance task outside the bundle still blocks as before.

decisions.id: D5 FR-006 bundle as the task
decisions.summary: One builder serves one bundle. The resume refusal after landing still fires because the landing ticks every member, whichever member's id the guard reads. The context-cap guard is unchanged.
decisions.why: This is an exception to FR-006's 'serves one task'. The GM's words call for it: working the tiny tasks 'at the same time' with one builder is how the builder's reading-in cost is paid once, and that cost is one of the fixed costs bundling exists to cut. FR-006's purpose is to keep builder contexts small, and that is still enforced without change. The context threshold guard is untouched, and resuming a builder after its bundle lands is still refused, since every member is ticked. This ruling does not rest on the members being small: a large bundle reaches the same context cap as a large task.

decisions.summary: The event log files a T=a,b,c command under the first member, so the static-runs guard and the plan-round tripwire count a bundle once. PLAN_ROUND_CAP and STATIC_RUNS_A_TASK are unchanged.
decisions.why: A bundle gets the same allowance one task gets, which is tighter than n tasks would get, not a carve-out from FR-007 or the round cap.

decisions.summary: make where-time reports a bundle's time under its first member (performance checklist 5). The other members carry no time of their own.
decisions.why: One builder's minute, one closing run and one review round in a bundle belong to the bundle, not to any one member. No per-member split could be true. The time is kept whole, so the categories (tests, compile, gate, land, review) and the totals the retrospective tooling exists to show are intact. This is a difference in how the time is reported, not a wrong answer from the tool.

decisions.summary: A heading that opens with a list of task ids followed by (bundle), Approach, part B or Performance checklist belongs to every listed task. Any other list heading still belongs to its first task, which keeps feature 405's 15 existing headings as they were. The search space is stated: a grep of specs/*/plan*.md.
decisions.why: The bundle section needs this, and the plan does not change how past plans are read.

decisions.summary: make decide T=a,b,c is refused while a member's section is not the first member's, or while T= differs from the heading's list, and the refusal names the fix. The lint runs once and the checklist once per member. One MODE 4 prompt asks the reviewer to judge every task in the bundle.

decisions.why: One set of closing runs per bundle, which is the fixed cost the GM asked to pay once.

Block reviews, ticked tasks', absent features' and every other pass still refuse.

decisions.id: reach: the rule in the set all three refusals read

decisions.id: no escape added at the first pass
decisions.summary: cheap.rs asks --refuse --landing <feature> --tasks <ids>; LEDGER_ROWS_OK stays at the push and make land-tooling only.
decisions.why: The heading's second half is answered by removing the refusal the landing could not answer, rather than by adding a way past it. Its own session clears them with the named make ledger-owed WRITE= and a commit. The '70 still owed with the clone's 46 uncommitted rows added' sentence shows they are rows the session itself has not yet written, not rows a landing cannot reach. FR-012's escape rule covers FR-006 to 009, 011 and 013, not this ledger refusal that predates the feature.

decisions.id: found and left: the 86-133 untied passes
decisions.summary: The passes no subject ties to a feature (impl-drift DECIDE_OK dispatches, workflow units, modal and record checks) refuse every landing until the session writes and commits their rows; called working as designed, not filed.

decisions.summary: rows.rs gains wave_transcript to find <session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/agent-<id>.jsonl; session_of names a wave unit's session as the directory above subagents/workflows/<run>/; filled_row takes a wave unit's reply and label from its run's journal.jsonl result line and fills the same cells a hand-dispatched pass gets.

decisions.why: Within the task: the task line is the trace, and choosing which source fills the verdict cell, the same reading verdict_of already gives every hand-dispatched pass, narrows nothing asked. Whether an all-IN-STEP impl-drift reply reading 'findings' is a wrong outcome: the bundle shows none. The plan's own constraint is that a row answers a pass by its check and cost cells (feature 371), and nothing in the bundle shows a consumer of the verdict cell that would refuse, let through or misreport work because of it. It is a pre-existing reading of verdict_of shared by the hand-dispatched rows, not introduced here; on what the bundle shows it is a difference, not a defect left (constitution XIV), so it needs no ruling.

decisions.summary: settle::settled / cost::subagent_files are not taught the wave directory, so a wave pass keeps the hook's logged cost cells rather than cells recomputed from its finished transcript; the size of any difference was not measured.

The plan states the unmeasured size of the gap openly rather than claiming it is nil.

decisions.summary: The fix's binary runs make ledger-owed WRITE= with the session's earlier rows' full text, writing 41 rows (the 35 impl-drift units and 6 later passes), with the 40 plan reviews refused as their landings' own per 451 T105; after, only 40 MODE 4 plan reviews are owed.
decisions.why: Carrying out the task's goal under an existing rule (451 T105); the WRITE= text names where every check's verdict is recorded, so applying it to the 6 later passes asserts nothing false. Nothing asked is narrowed.

decisions.summary: Red-first pins in ledger_passes/tests.rs (a wave unit written for its own session from the journal, another session's unit left owed) and rows/tests.rs (text result, structured result without text, no result, no agent), shown red before the fix; then crate tests, lint, cover, closing checks.
decisions.why: Tests whose only effect is to make the requested fix happen and keep happening; enforcement of the task, not added scope.

decisions.summary: transcript( callers under rust/gate/crates/reviews found by grep; trace.rs unit_prompt already walks the wave directory and is unchanged; cost::transcript itself is not changed.
decisions.why: The enumeration states its search space; because the fix adds wave_transcript in rows.rs rather than changing cost::transcript, callers of cost::transcript outside that crate are not affected. No narrowing.

decisions.summary: The plan declares no defect found and left.
decisions.why: Consistent with the rulings above: the verdict-cell reading is shown by the bundle to be a difference with no wrong outcome, and the cost-cell limitation is a stated, purpose-justified choice, not a defect shown. Nothing else in the block is left.

decisions.summary: T151 is declared not performance work for FR-013's scheduling.
decisions.why: The task repairs the review ledger's tracing of check-wave passes to their session so landings stop being refused; it neither improves a measured time nor is the time-measurement work the GM asked on 2026-11-20 to count as performance. The declaration takes nothing from FR-013.

decisions.summary: One Phase line form (phase_row in event_log_hooks.rs) built in one place, every writer appending through append_row_with, the hooks' writer; the make target read one way via shared::make::outermost_goal
decisions.why: FR-003/D4 name the hooks' line writer as the one writer; a shared form is how every step the GM named gets measured the same way.

decisions.summary: hookrun.sh leaves each job's span and make hooks-test hands them to the door in one call, so closing-checks and make done write theirs too

decisions.summary: make record, quick, preflight, cohort timed whole by the Makefile's TIMED macro (quick's checks moved to _quick)

decisions.summary: Page sessions write write/check lines from the runner, booked under their task directly since no Bash run holds them
decisions.why: Detached work that was invisible is now measured and attributed rather than left loose.

decisions.summary: where_time/columns.rs books each phase to compile, hook suites, map generation, tests, gate, docs or review; containers book none; Split carves categories in a fixed order so parallel suites count once; both tables gain hook suites and map generation columns; a session-less test phase is now counted loose

decisions.why: Narrows the split the readers give, not the measurement: the lines are written and the seconds remain counted in the run's FR-001 bucket, so nothing is invisible. Splitting clippy into compile vs tests is not possible without a seam inside one process, and rustfmt is neither, so booking either to compile or tests would misstate the very categories the GM wants to read; the literal alternative defeats the request's purpose (accurate knowledge of where time goes).

decisions.summary: Lines verified by real runs in the clone for map, cohort, record, quick, page session and hook suites; make preflight and make done's gate phases shown by unit tests (runstats/tests.rs) alone until a make done runs
decisions.why: The writers for those steps are implemented as asked; this is how their working is shown, not a reduction of what is measured, and the plan states it plainly rather than claiming a run.

decisions.summary: T147's left rule widened from plan reviews to every non-plan-review pass, read by a new left/whose.rs, through the one owed set the first pass, the push's row and make land-tooling all read
decisions.why: The task line names a landing refused on other started tasks' record and pop-up check passes. Widening to every non-plan-review pass does not drop a row: each left pass is still owed by its own task's landing or session, and the refusal stays on everything not attributable to another started, unticked task. No GM clause or FR touches the ledger refusal, so this narrows nothing asked.

decisions.summary: Whose a pass is: first source naming a task, in own.rs's order - own words (logged subject, check-bundle -t<n> suffix, meta description), then builder (parentAgentId's brief), then page session (index.txt brief's feature and first-line task, else file name); prompt bodies never read
decisions.why: A design of the attribution the task needs, grounded in a dated measurement (25 of 26 named by page session, 1 by builder) and in the measured fact that prompt bodies name unrelated tasks. Implements the task; narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: A bare task id takes the feature that started it (event_log_hooks::started); a number names its unique specs/<n>-*
decisions.why: Resolution detail needed to attribute a pass; carries no carve-out from the task line.

decisions.summary: A pass is left only where its task is STARTED (task-starts.jsonl), not merely open
decisions.why: The task line itself says 'other started tasks''. An open task nobody started has no landing or session coming to write the row, so leaving its pass would lose the row.

decisions.summary: A pass of a ticked task (in tasks.md or tasks-done.md) still refuses, though task-starts.jsonl records it as started
decisions.why: The task line's 'started tasks' are tasks whose own landings and sessions will write their rows; a ticked task's landing has already happened, so leaving its pass would leave the row unwritten forever, defeating the ledger. task-starts.jsonl keeps every landed task's start (740 rows), so 'started' alone would leave almost everything. No known instance is left: the after-measurement refuses 3 passes, all the landing's own. A hypothetical refusal is not a known defect left.

decisions.summary: A pass naming a task never started still refuses
decisions.why: Outside the task line (not a started task), no landing or session is coming to write it, and the after-measurement shows no such pass in today's owed set: no known defect left.

decisions.summary: A pass whose every source names no task still refuses every landing until its session writes its row (found and left, judged working as designed, not filed)
decisions.why: Not a pass of another started task, so outside the task line; no landing can know whose it is, and leaving it would let an unattributable pass escape the ledger. None of the 26 measured owed passes named nothing (all were attributed), and the after-measurement's 3 refusals are the landing's own, so no known instance is left unfixed.

decisions.summary: The landing's own passes, by any source, bare or with its feature, still refuse with make ledger-owed WRITE= named
decisions.why: The task line is about OTHER tasks' passes; the landing's own are writable by WRITE= as the landing session's, so refusing them is the existing behavior the task leaves intact.

decisions.summary: Plan-review passes keep T147's rule unchanged
decisions.why: The task line names record and pop-up check passes; plan reviews are T147's already-settled case.

decisions.summary: 449 T258's own.rs is not reused as code (it lives in l7r_guard, which no gate crate may name per check guard-deps); whose.rs reads the same sources after the fact from l7r_shared, regexes copied; no guard source edited
decisions.why: Implementation choice forced by the T66 crate rule; same sources and order, no change to what the task delivers.

decisions.summary: Transcripts listed once per refusal (settle::Transcripts made pub(super) and shared), only for passes whose subject names no task
decisions.why: Cost choice inside the task; attribution unchanged.

decisions.summary: note() reworded to 'the passes of N open task(s) left to their own landings and sessions (451 T147, T157), which write their rows'; T147's pins follow
decisions.why: Message follows the widened rule; narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The heading's note that LEDGER_ROWS_OK does not reach the first pass is not addressed; the escape's reach stays as it is (unlabeled by the author)
decisions.why: The task line's subject is the landing refused on other tasks' passes; the escape's reach is given as why that refusal had no way out. Once the first pass refuses only passes the running session can write (WRITE=), the way out exists, and the after-measurement shows the observed refusal cleared. No request clause or FR asks for the escape to reach the first pass, and no remaining refusal without a remedy is known.

decisions.summary: Two pins (left/tests.rs reading test, land inproc.rs first-pass test), each shown red with clues.left_to stubbed
decisions.why: Enforcement of the task's own behavior (FR-012's red-first practice); serves the task, not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: T98 is a measurement of builder-slot occupancy under T88's rolling dispatch; no engine or hook code changes and L7R_BUILDERS stays at 3.
decisions.why: A measurement task of the builders' loop, counted as performance work by FR-013 and the GM's 2026-11-20 words on measurement tasks; the measurement finds no wrong outcome to fix, so leaving the constant and code as they are narrows nothing.

decisions.summary: The night window runs from T88's landing (2026-11-21T18:40:16Z) to the last night builder's end (07:06Z), 745 minutes, and leaves out the 3-hour builder-free gap before T147.
decisions.why: Chosen by the same rule as T88's before window (the builders' day, first start to last end); the before is reproduced to the minute by the same script, so before and after are one method.

decisions.summary: Occupancy is reported both for 451's builders alone (the before's method) and for every feature's builders (what the Stop hook counts).
decisions.why: Reports more, hides nothing; the before has no 449 builder so its row is the same in both readings.

decisions.summary: The replay's independent-task rule (a line naming no file a running task edits) is kept although it does not read 'after T<n>' and so over-reports for the 449-slot minutes.
decisions.why: Kept so before and after are one method, and the over-report is disclosed with its cause; a difference of method that is stated, not a defect left.

decisions.summary: The stretches below three are attributed to a recorded choice to give the slot to 449 when no 451 task could start, to landings, and to 30-80 s dispatch latency; the Stop hook's count is found correct for the window, and nothing is fixed.
decisions.why: Each cause is named with its source; none is a wrong outcome (the weekly cap and T156's miscount are each ruled out with evidence), so there is no known defect carried past this task.

decisions.summary: T98 runs after T88 and a full day, and before T22.
decisions.why: Ordering inside the feature's own task list; narrows nothing the GM asked.

decisions.summary: builder_brief reads the feature number and every task id before the description's first colon, words between allowed; a range T289-T300 is each member at its first id's width; a backwards, lettered or wider-than-SPAN range reads as its two ends.
decisions.why: A defect fix in this feature's rolling-dispatch tooling (451 T88, the bundling the GM asked for 2026-11-22, T141): the Stop hook miscounted five live builders. Fixing a known bug as found is the standing rule; a malformed range kept to its two ends is the prior behavior, not a narrowing of anything asked.

decisions.summary: A running agent whose description names a landing before its colon, or whose prompt's first line runs make land (not land-tooling/land-stop), is a lander; free_slot names no task-start while one runs. A landing brief naming neither reads as no lander, failing toward a visibly named start.
decisions.why: Carries the arbiter's ruling ask:set-down-449-mid-landing (no task-start while a landing runs) into the hook. The residual case (an unrecognizable landing brief) is backed by (c)'s process check for any landing actually running in the clone, and fails toward a named start the session can see rather than a hidden hold; the ruling binds the session's conduct, which a named suggestion does not override. No requested behavior is cut.

decisions.summary: A landing process in this clone or its -land worktree (l7r-gate land without --stop, or land-alone.sh), found by walking /proc (L7R_PROC_ROOT in tests), also holds the slots; the few lines of the land crate's landing_pids shape are re-read here rather than imported.
decisions.why: Same ruling, enforced on the process rather than the brief; where the code lives is design, not fidelity.

decisions.summary: next_independent skips a running builder's own tasks, including bundle members never task-started, so none is named the next start.
decisions.why: A defect found while testing and fixed in the task (fix as we go); it makes the hook's start-next correct for the bundles the GM asked for.

decisions.summary: SPAN = 200, a CONVENTION past the widest bundle seen (twelve).
decisions.why: A labeled convention bounding range expansion; it narrows nothing asked, and a range beyond it keeps the old two-ends reading.

decisions.summary: Green on make rust-test CRATE=rust/guard/shared, its cover, lint, format and the hook suite; red recorded and the task set down, a cannot-be-done claim ruled through make arbiter-ask; red-first tests for the three new cases.
decisions.why: Verification of the fix itself; enforcement of the requested behavior, not unrequested scope.

decisions.summary: Nothing left: the one defect found (range members named as next start) is fixed here.
decisions.why: No defect is deferred.

decisions.summary: Every rule lives in the existing scratch-sweep guard, so the cache has one cleaner.
decisions.why: Where the cleanup lives is how it is built, not how much of it there is. It serves 'clean up after ourselves in terms of the file system' and drops nothing.

decisions.summary: make done, make land and make closing-checks refuse below L7R_DISK_FLOOR_GB (15, GUESS) free. The refusal names the largest build directories, what cache-clean would free, the scratch worktrees and the DISK_OK escape, which is recorded.
decisions.why: This is the 'without us realizing it' half of the GM's words, enforced: a gate stops before the disk fills. The recorded escape is the project's standing guard rule. 15 is a knob marked GUESS, and the 4.56/24.77/31 GB figures that back it each carry a date and a method.

decisions.summary: make cache-clean [DRY=1] [HOURS=n] takes the cache's share of the sweep once idle past 12 h (GUESS). It is refused while any cargo/rustc/clippy/llvm-cov process runs, and a build directory a live process or a live run member holds is kept whole.
decisions.why: This is the cleanup the GM asked for. Not deleting under a running build is a physical constraint: deleting there would corrupt it and force the cold rebuild the GM's 'reusing the same build cache' point warns against. The floor still catches a machine that is never idle. The machine-wide refusal is broader than the per-target in_use check strictly needs, but that is a design choice and not a fidelity matter.

decisions.summary: A build directory is live when its name belongs to a clone, the mirror, a clone's -land/-tooling/-land-tooling, or a registered worktree whose tree exists. Because four worktrees share 'wt', its cache stays while any of them exists.
decisions.why: This fixes a measured defect, the old rule judging 'wt' dead, and keeps the cache that live work reuses, which is the GM's stated intention.

decisions.summary: A build directory goes whole only when no code path builds into its name AND every tree its dep-info names is gone. One with no dep-info cannot be proven dead and is kept. rc, clone and tree are kept; head is taken.
decisions.why: It narrows the cleanup: some directories that may be dead are kept. The GM's own words imply the exception: 'your points about reusing the same build cache and whatnot are well taken... you have correctly understood my intention'. The measured case shows what the literal reading would do. Presumed-dead deletion would have taken rc (11 GB, a live scratch clone's checks target) plus clone and tree, which current code builds into, and that is the cold-rebuild cost the GM accepted as a reason. The purpose ('not have 30 gigs... eaten without us realizing it') is still met for what is kept, because the floor refuses and names the largest build directories, live or dead. The exception covers three cases, ruled separately: (a) a name a code path builds into is reused by construction, so legitimate; (b) a tree its dep-info names still exists is live by evidence, so legitimate; (c) no dep-info, so nothing to prove from, kept and surfaced by the floor's listing, legitimate on the same 'no loss of the cache' ground and bounded by the floor.

decisions.summary: Keep each crate's newest SIXTEEN variants, not four, restating the task line's 'the newest per crate' as a count. KEPT 4 -> 16.
decisions.why: It keeps more than the task line's literal 'newest' would. Applied literally, that rule defeats the purpose the GM endorsed, reusing the build cache. It was measured: one landing gate touched 13 live l7r_mode_a variants, so keeping one or four takes variants a live build is using and forces rebuilds. The size budget still takes every variant past sixteen when the cache is over 100 GB, and the floor still refuses, so the GM's 'without us realizing it' purpose is not gutted. The task line is the session's wording, not the GM's; the GM's words do not fix a count.

decisions.summary: Past L7R_CACHE_BUDGET_GB (100, GUESS), the cleanup and the day's sweep take every dead tree's directory and every variant past sixteen, whatever its age. They never take one in use and never run while a build runs.
decisions.why: This adds cleanup in service of the request. The 100 GB knob is marked GUESS and is backed by dated du figures.

decisions.summary: The day's sweep removes this uid's /tmp/t<N>... and /tmp/tmp.* idle past 24 h (GUESS), and session task outputs idle past 24 h, a live session's included. A held-open output, and an entry holding a registered worktree, stay.
decisions.why: This is file-system cleanup the GM asked for. Keeping files that are held open or that hold a worktree prevents breaking live work; it is not a carve-out from 'clean up'. The 24 h split carries the host's dated measurement.

decisions.summary: A session's first prompt starts the sweep. The plan hooks it on the same UserPromptSubmit event that clone-sync uses, but from the sweep's own guard rather than from a call inside clone_sync_hooks. The plan labels this a deviation from the task line's '(the clone-sync prompt hook)'.
decisions.why: Ruled as the plan asks. It narrows nothing: the trigger is the same (a session's first prompt), the effect is the same (the sweep starts however recent the day's sweep was), and only the file the call sits in differs. No case the task line covers goes unswept, so it is not an exception and needs no ruling. Keeping the period, lock and detached start in one place is a placement choice. The GM asked for the cleanup, not for its host module.

decisions.summary: After a successful make land, the landed tasks' /tmp/t<N>* are removed. When another feature started a task of the same number within the day, removal is left to the 24 h age rule, and the plan says so.
decisions.why: The cleanup still happens, by the age rule within a day, so nothing is left uncleaned. Removing at once would delete another feature's live scratch (measured: 449 T158 and 451 T158 share /tmp/t158), which is destroying work, not cleaning up after ourselves.

decisions.summary: A scratch worktree is removed only when it is idle 24 h, not held, its HEAD is on a ref, and git worktree remove takes it without --force. Every other worktree is named with its idle hours, its build directory and the --force command, not removed. The plan labels this decision.
decisions.why: It narrows the cleanup: dirty or ref-less idle worktrees, and their build directories, which stay live through the registered-name rule, are named rather than removed. Removing a worktree with uncommitted files or a commit no ref holds destroys work that cannot be recovered. 'Clean up after ourselves' does not reach that, and the plan records that it cannot tell which task made a worktree, so it cannot tell whether anyone still wants it. The earlier review's concern, 'naming is an instruction, not the cleanup', is answered two ways. Every worktree that can be removed without loss now is removed. And the rest is not left to an instruction: the floor refuses done/land/closing-checks and names them, so 'without us realizing it' holds as real enforcement.

decisions.summary: The scratch-sweep guard's unit tests now use fixture paths for the cache, clones, mirror and /tmp, not the machine's real ones. This fixes the real worktree /tmp/t216/wt that a test removed.
decisions.why: This fixes a defect found in the task, an instance of the cleanup reaching real data. It is fixed here and not deferred.

decisions.summary: The clone's guard build link failure was fixed by hand (tool-profile artifacts and incremental sessions removed, rebuilt). No rule is added because its cause is not proven.

Whether to file a follow-up on builder builds is scheduling, not a fidelity question for this section.

decisions.summary: A fresh tree's coverage run is red on rust/mode_a (armory test reads two .gitignored generated SVGs, NotFound). Not fixed here; filed as T159, ordered to land before T148.
decisions.why: This is a defect (a check that refuses good work in a new tree), so leaving it unfixed in this task is a narrowing and is ruled on. It is legitimate: the section is a trial that changes no code, the defect is not dropped but filed as T159 with a stated reason and a stated order ('lands before T148', the first task that builds in fresh trees, so the defect cannot bite before it is fixed), which meets FR-009's form. Fix-as-we-go asks that a step's known defects be fixed before the next step begins, and that order does exactly that.

decisions.summary: T155 is run as a trial: measure a landing's duplicate build and two candidates (sccache, building at the clone's path), no code changed.

decisions.summary: Verdict (a): no content-keyed compilation cache is built, because it hit 0 times across the two paths, coverage units are uncacheable under it, and 0.13 has no base-directory option.
decisions.why: The task's own goal (Approach item 1: a landing compiles nothing the clone already compiled) is left unmet by this candidate, so it is a narrowing; but the candidate is measured to be physically unable to deliver: 0 hits at the second path, every coverage unit 'multiple input files', and even with a base-directory option the ceiling is rlibs only, bought with CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 in every builder's loop, which would slow the loop the GM asked to speed. Physically impossible as it stands, not merely awkward.

decisions.summary: Verdict (b): the landing is not built at the clone's path in the clone's target directory, because mtime freshness across two trees reuses the clone's build of a different copy - a red tree passed cover clean.
decisions.why: Adjudicated separately from (a). Building it would defeat the request's own purpose: the GM asked for performance improvements and for enforcement that is real, and a landing whose tests run the clone builders' code instead of the commit's is a check that passes bad work - a defect, measured on a deliberate hazard (red probe passes at the clone's path, fails in its own directory).
